content: Precision refers to the alteration in the orientation of the axis of a rotating object. In physics, there are two types of precession: torque-free and torque-induced. This discussion focuses on torque-induced precession. In some contexts, precession may describe the precession experienced by Earth, its effects on astronomical observations, or the precession of orbital objects. Torque-Free Precession Torque-free precession occurs when the axis of rotation deviates slightly from the axis about which the object can rotate stably. Poinsot's construction is a geometrical method used to visualize the torque-free motion of a rotating rigid body. For instance, when a plate is thrown, it may rotate around an axis that is not its axis of symmetry. In non-perfectly solid objects, internal vortices tend to dampen torque-free precession. For example, a part of a gyroscope wobbles when torque is applied. This phenomenon is commonly observed in spinning toy tops, but all rotating objects can undergo precession. If the rotational speed and the magnitude of the torque remain constant, the axis of rotation will describe a cone, moving at right angles to the direction of the applied torque. In the case of a toy top, if the axis is not perfectly vertical, gravity applies a torque that tends to tip it over. Gimbal-Mounted Devices A gimbal-mounted device consists of three axes of rotation: the hub of the wheel, the gimbal axis, and the vertical pivot. To differentiate between the two horizontal axes, rotation around the wheel hub is termed rolling, while rotation around the gimbal axis is called pitching. Rotation around the pivot axis is referred to as spinning. Imagine the device spinning around the pivot axis, with some rolling motion added. If the gimbal axis is locked, preventing pitching, sensors on the gimbal axis measure any torque around it. When rolling begins, a section of the wheel (e.g., dm1) at the perimeter of the spinning motion has significant velocity. As it is forced closer to the center of rotation, it moves in the direction of the top-left arrow in the diagram (at 45° in the direction of rolling). Another section of the wheel (e.g., dm2) starts at the center of rotation with zero velocity. A force is required to increase dm2's velocity to match the perimeter velocity. If this force is not provided, dm2's inertia causes it to move in the direction of the top-right arrow. Both arrows point in the same direction. The same reasoning applies to the bottom half of the wheel, but the arrows point in the opposite direction. Combined over the entire wheel, a torque arises around the gimbal axis when rolling is added to vertical-axis rotation. This torque occurs instantaneously, without delay. Gyroscopic Precession In a spinning top, when it tilts, gravity exerts a torque. Instead of rolling over, the top pitches, reorienting itself with respect to the applied torque. This results in gyroscopic precession, where gravity's torque causes the top to precess rather than fall over. Gyroscopic precession also affects high-speed bicycle performance, gyroscopic compasses, and helicopter flight controls. In helicopters, the rotor disk's rotation introduces gyroscopic precession. For example, tilting the rotor disk forward for forward velocity requires the downward net force on the blade to be applied approximately 90° earlier (depending on blade configuration). Corrective linkages in the aircraft adjust the blade pitch in advance of the blade's position relative to the swashplate, ensuring the pilot's inputs are accurate. Classical (Newtonian) Precession Classical precession results from the interaction between the angular velocity of rotation and the angular velocity produced by torque. This angular velocity occurs about a line that forms an angle with the permanent rotation axis, lying in a plane perpendicular to the torque-producing couple. The permanent axis must turn toward this line, as the body cannot continue rotating about a line that is not a principal axis of maximum moment of inertia. If the rotating body is symmetric and unconstrained, and the torque on the spin axis is perpendicular to that axis, the precession axis will be perpendicular to both the spin axis and the torque axis. The angular velocity of precession is given by: [ boldsymbol{omega}_p = frac{Q}{I_s boldsymbol{omega}_s} ] where (I_s) is the moment of inertia, (boldsymbol{omega}_s) is the angular velocity of spin about the spin axis, and (Q) is the torque. Using (boldsymbol{omega} = frac{2pi}{T}), the period of precession is: [ T_p = frac{4pi^2 I_s}{Q T_s} ] where (T_s) is the period of spin about the spin axis. In general, the problem is more complex than this simplified explanation. Relativistic Precession Relativity introduces three types of corrections to Newtonian precession for a gyroscope near a large mass, such as Earth: 1. Thomas Precession: A special relativistic correction accounting for the observer being in a rotating non-inertial frame. 2. De Sitter Precession: A general relativistic correction due to the Schwarzschild metric of curved space near a large non-rotating mass. 3. Lense-Thirring Precession: A general relativistic correction due to frame-dragging by the Kerr metric of curved space near a large rotating mass. Earth's Axial Precession Earth undergoes a complete precession cycle approximately every 25,800 years, causing the positions of stars in the equatorial coordinate system to change slowly. This shift is due to the change in coordinates, not the stars themselves. The discovery of the precession of the equinoxes is attributed to the ancient Greek astronomer Hipparchus, though Aristarchus of Samos noted the difference between sidereal and tropical years earlier. Newtonian physics later explained this phenomenon. Earth's oblate spheroid shape, with an equatorial bulge, experiences gravitational tidal forces from the Moon and Sun, which apply torque to align the bulge with the ecliptic plane. This is known as lunisolar precession. Planetary orbits also exhibit precession. The major axis of a planet's elliptical orbit precesses within its orbital plane due to gravitational perturbations from other planets. This is called perihelion precession or apsidal precession. Discrepancies in Mercury's observed perihelion precession rate, compared to classical mechanics predictions, were key evidence supporting Einstein's Theory of Relativity, which accurately predicted these anomalies. Periodic changes in Earth's orbital parameters, combined with axial precession and inclination changes, are integral to the astronomical theory of ice ages. Similar phenomena include lunar precession and nodal precession, which affect the orientation of orbital planes.
